population.short: Every unit you want to describe. Here it is exactly the rows of your chosen CSV: a fixed, finite list you can count.
population.more: Because the whole population is in the file, you can calculate its true mean and check every sampling method against it. That luxury is why this is a teaching exercise: in real work the population is usually too large or costly to measure completely. Your file is not all patients, all clinics or all days.

unit.short: The thing one row describes: one appointment, one person, or one recorded minute. Samples are sets of units.
unit.more: Saying what one row means stops you from mixing up, for example, the average per appointment with the average per patient or per day.

target.short: The column whose average you are estimating, such as wait_time, charges or heart_rate_bpm. Always state its units.

true-mean.short: The average of the target over every row of the population. It is fixed: it does not change from sample to sample.
true-mean.more: Changing the population's values or which rows it contains may change its true mean, so recalculate it whenever they change. Reordering the same rows does not change it.

sample.short: The subset of rows a sampling method selects. Its size is n.
sample.more: A sample is one draw. Two samples of the same size from the same method usually differ.

sample-size.short: How many rows are in one sample. N (capital) is the number of rows in the population.
sample-size.more: Comparisons between methods are fair only when every method uses the same n.

estimate.short: A number calculated from a sample to stand in for an unknown population value, here the sample's estimate of the true mean.
estimate.more: One estimate comes from one sample. Whether a method is trustworthy is judged by how its estimates behave over many samples, not by one result.

sample-mean.short: The plain average of the target over the sampled rows. It is the estimate for simple random and systematic sampling.

without-replacement.short: A row can be selected at most once in a sample, so a sample of n contains n different rows.

seed.short: A starting number for the random number generator. The same seed and settings reproduce the same results, so you and others can check them.
seed.more: Record the seed with every piece of random-sampling evidence. Compare several seeds to see whether your conclusion is stable. Exact enumeration involves no random draws, so it does not depend on a seed.

srs.short: Choose n rows without replacement so that every possible set of n rows is equally likely.
srs.more: Each row has the same chance of selection, n/N. The sample mean is the estimate.

systematic.short: Take every k-th row in the file's order, beginning at a random start. With N rows and sample size n, the interval is k = N/n.
systematic.more: When N/n is a whole number, use the whole-number interval: there are only k possible samples, one for each start. When it is not, use the fractional-interval design (start u on (0, k], rows ceil(u + j·k)). Both give exactly n distinct rows and the same chance n/N for every row. What the method sees depends on the row order.

sampling-interval.short: The step between selected rows in systematic sampling: k = N/n. With N = 10,000 and n = 100, k = 100.

random-start.short: The randomly chosen first row of a systematic sample, between 1 and k. It is the only random step: once it is chosen, every other selected row is fixed.
random-start.more: Because of the random start, every row still has the same chance of being selected, so systematic sampling is a probability sample.

row-order.short: The sequence of rows in the file. Systematic sampling walks through it, so its meaning matters: time order in a clinic log or a wearable record, but only file order in an unordered list of people.
row-order.more: In the heart-rate file, rows are in time order but minutes with no reading are missing, so row number and clock time are not the same thing.

stratified.short: Split the population into groups (strata) using a column you can observe, take a simple random sample within each group, then combine the group means with population weights.
stratified.more: The allocation says how many rows come from each stratum; it must total n and cannot exceed any stratum's size.

stratum.short: One group in stratified sampling, defined by an observable column such as visit_type, age_band or activity_state. Every row belongs to exactly one stratum.

allocation.short: How the total sample size n is split among strata. Proportional allocation gives each stratum about n × N_h / N rows, rounded to whole numbers that still total n.
allocation.more: Rounding needs a rule (for example, largest remainder) and a check that no stratum is asked for more rows than it has, and that each stratum gets at least one.

weighting.short: The stratified estimate is Σ (N_h / N) × (sample mean in stratum h): each group's mean counts in proportion to that group's share of the population.
weighting.more: Averaging all sampled rows together only matches this when the allocation is exactly proportional. Getting the weights wrong is a calculation error, not a failure of stratification.

inclusion-probability.short: The chance that a particular row ends up in the sample. In SRS and systematic sampling with a random start, it is n/N for every row.

repeated-sampling.short: Drawing many samples with the same method, size, settings and population, and keeping every estimate together, labelled with its settings, to see how the method behaves rather than how one draw turned out.
repeated-sampling.more: The repetition count is separate from the sample size n: at n = 10 with 100 repetitions, you draw 100 separate samples of 10 observations and get 100 sample means. Each sample is drawn without replacement; an observation may appear again in a later repetition. Keep each experiment's estimates as its own set. Never pool estimates from different populations, conditions, methods, settings or sample sizes.

sampling-distribution.short: The spread of estimates a method produces across repeated samples. Its centre shows bias; its width shows variability.

monte-carlo.short: Approximating a sampling distribution by drawing many random samples (here at least 100 by default, with the option to increase to 1,000). Results vary with the seed, so label them Monte Carlo.
monte-carlo.more: 100 repetitions usually reveal the main pattern; 1,000 give smoother distributions and more stable bias, SD and RMSE estimates. Neither guarantees stable results, and more repetitions do not change how good the method itself is. Rerun with different seeds to check whether your main conclusions hold.

exact-enumeration.short: Listing every possible sample instead of drawing random ones. Systematic sampling with a whole-number interval k has only k possible samples (one per random start), so all k can be listed.
exact-enumeration.more: With N = 10,000 and n = 100 there are exactly 100 possible systematic samples, each with probability 1/100. The result is exact: it uses no random draws and does not depend on a seed. Label it exact, not Monte Carlo. For this activity, use exact enumeration for whole-number systematic sampling and Monte Carlo for the other required results.

bias.short: The average of a method's estimates minus the true mean, in the target's units. It is a consistent error in one direction, seen across many samples.
bias.more: One estimate that misses the true mean is not evidence of bias. A Monte Carlo bias is usually not exactly zero even for an unbiased method: it may be simulation noise, it is not guaranteed to be small, and its sign can change from seed to seed. Compare several seeds before calling it real bias.

variability.short: How much a method's estimates differ from sample to sample. Usually summarised as the standard deviation (SD) of the estimates: √(average of (estimate − mean of estimates)²).
variability.more: This SD describes how repeated estimates spread, not how individual values in the population spread. A method can be unbiased but highly variable (right on average, often far off), or have low variability but be biased (consistent, but consistently off).

rmse.short: √(average of (estimate − true mean)²) over repeated samples, in the target's units: the typical size of the estimation error.
rmse.more: It accounts for both bias and variability: RMSE² = bias² + SD², when the SD divides by the number of repetitions.

standard-error.short: The standard deviation of an estimate across repeated samples. In this activity you measure it directly as the SD of your repeated estimates.

baseline.short: The supplied population, in its supplied order, with the default settings. Every changed condition is compared against it.

modified-population.short: A labelled copy of the population with values, membership or row order changed by the user. Its true mean must be recalculated; the original stays recoverable.

plan-mode.short: An agent mode for discussion only: the agent proposes and compares options but does not edit files or run changing commands.
plan-mode.more: You switch it yourself. In Claude Code, press Shift+Tab until the status line shows plan mode. In Cursor or VS Code with GitHub Copilot, choose Plan in the chat's mode or agent picker. Other tools: check their documentation.

implementation-mode.short: Any agent mode that may edit files and run commands, used after you have chosen a design. For example, Claude Code's default or accept-edits mode, or Agent in Cursor or VS Code with GitHub Copilot.

agent-brief.short: The starter file your agent reads first: the task, the sampling rules, the mode workflow and its boundaries.

decisions-md.short: Your own notes file: population, design choices, results table, findings, challenge hypothesis, interpretation and AI use. You write it; your agent does not.
